hotspot.description: Standing tall before you is a Bunya Pine, a species that has been a part of the Queensland landscape since the era of the dinosaurs. These particular trees were among the first "ornamental" plantings in the gardens, dating back to the mid-19th century. To the local Indigenous people, the Bunya was—and is—sacred; its massive cones, which can weigh up to 10kg, provided a vital food source and a reason for large gatherings. Today, they serve as majestic sentinels, watching over the transition from the city's historic past to its modern skyline.
hotspot.title: The Ancient Giants of the Gardens

hotspot.description:
Naval Stores is a heritage-listed storehouse at 34 Amesbury Street, Kangaroo Point, Queensland, Australia. It was built from 1886 to 1900s. It is also known as Naval Brigade Stores and Naval Depot. It was added to the Queensland Heritage Register on 21 October 1992.[1]
Brisbane-based adventure company, Riverlife Adventure Centre, operates from the Naval Stores premises.
hotspot.title: Naval Stores, Kangaroo Point

hotspot.description: Completed in 1889, this heritage icon stands as a grand reminder of Brisbane’s history as a major colonial port. Designed in the Victorian Free Classical style, its most famous feature is the massive copper-sheathed dome and the grand Corinthian columns facing the river. Originally built to collect duties on goods entering the city, the building was meticulously restored by the University of Queensland and now serves as one of Brisbane's premier cultural and dining venues.
hotspot.title: Customs House: A Victorian Masterpiece

hotspot.description: You are standing in the heart of what was once a forgotten industrial site. Originally constructed in the 1930s as a relief work project during the Great Depression, these wharves served the Howard Smith Co. shipping line for decades before falling into disuse. In 2018, the 3.4-hectare site was transformed into a world-class lifestyle precinct. The development carefully preserved the heritage-listed timber sheds and air-raid shelters while adding modern green spaces, a boutique hotel carved into the cliffside, and a cantilevered riverwalk that seamlessly connects the City to New Farm.
hotspot.title: Howard Smith Wharves: A Precinct Reimagined

hotspot.description: Completed in 1940, the Story Bridge is the largest steel cantilever bridge in Australia and the defining landmark of the Brisbane skyline. Designed by Dr. John Bradfield—the same mastermind behind the Sydney Harbour Bridge—it was built almost entirely of Australian materials during the Great Depression. Spanning 777 meters, it connects the high cliffs of Kangaroo Point to the valley and the city reach. More than just a transport link, the bridge is a protected heritage icon that has watched Brisbane grow from a quiet river town into a modern Olympic city.
hotspot.title: The Story Bridge: Brisbane’s Steel Sentinel

hotspot.description: You are standing on one of Brisbane’s most iconic pieces of modern infrastructure. After the original floating walkway was destroyed in the 2011 floods, this state-of-the-art replacement was engineered to withstand the river's power. It sits as a structural "bridge" over the water, separated from the shore to protect the riverbank. This 870-meter pathway provides a seamless, car-free link between the bustling Howard Smith Wharves and the quiet, historic charm of the New Farm peninsula.
hotspot.title: The New Farm Riverwalk: Engineering on the Water

hotspot.description: You are standing in a piece of living history. This marina was once the Evans Deakin Shipyard, which became one of Australia’s largest shipbuilding sites during World War II. Originally built in 1884 as Moar’s Slip, the site was expanded in 1940 to build naval corvettes, frigates, and massive cargo ships for the Allied war effort. Between 1940 and 1976, 81 ships were launched from these banks. The most famous was the Robert Miller—the largest ship ever built on the Brisbane River—which spectacularly broke free during the 1974 floods while still under construction. Today, the dry dock’s original footprint serves as the Dockside Marina, blending maritime heritage with modern luxury.
hotspot.title: Evans Deakin Dry Dock: The Birthplace of Giants

hotspot.description: Constructed in 1926, this imposing red-brick edifice originally served as a coal-fired power station for Brisbane’s vast tram network. After the trams were decommissioned in 1969, the building sat abandoned for decades, becoming a legendary space for squatters and graffiti artists. In 2000, it was reborn as a premier contemporary arts center. The renovation famously preserved its "industrial ruins" aesthetic—retaining heritage-listed graffiti and soot-stained walls—while integrating modern glass and steel to create a unique home for theater, comedy, and riverside festivals.
hotspot.title: Brisbane Powerhouse: From Industrial Hub to Cultural Icon

hotspot.description: From this vantage point above the City Botanic Gardens, you can see why Brisbane is known for its subtropical charm. Established in 1828 as a colonial food garden, these 18 hectares are now a lush sanctuary in the heart of the CBD. Following the river downstream will lead you past the iconic Story Bridge and Howard Smith Wharves toward the leafy, bohemian streets of New Farm. Whether you’re here for the 260+ days of sunshine or the thriving arts scene, Brisbane perfectly blends big-city energy with a relaxed, outdoor lifestyle.
hotspot.title: Welcome to Brisbane: The River City

hotspot.description: Established in 1914, New Farm Park is one of Brisbane’s oldest and most loved suburban retreats. This 15-hectare riverfront site has a layered history: it began as a convict farm in the 1820s, served as a world-class racecourse in the mid-1800s, and even hosted a US Navy submarine base during WWII. Today, it is famous for its centerpiece Rose Gardens, featuring over 2,500 bushes, and its massive, heritage-listed Moreton Bay Fig trees. Whether you are arriving by CityCat or walking the riverfront path from the Powerhouse, the park remains the "green lung" of the inner city and a premier spot for Brisbane’s outdoor lifestyle.
hotspot.title: New Farm Park: The Grand Peninsula

hotspot.description: From 120 meters above Mowbray Park, the geography of the "River City" is laid bare. Established in 1904, Mowbray Park is one of East Brisbane’s most historic green spaces, serving as a gateway between the city reaches and the southern suburbs. To your north, the river sweeps around the New Farm peninsula, while to the west, the Story Bridge and CBD skyline dominate the horizon. This vantage point perfectly illustrates why the river is the lifeblood of Brisbane—not just as a scenic backdrop, but as a winding highway that has shaped the city’s development for nearly two centuries.
hotspot.title: Mowbray Park: The Eagle's Eye View
